finding.headline: At 63 the 401(k) catch-up limit is higher, and Medicare starts at 65.
details: For 2027, employees aged 60 to 63 in these plans can contribute a catch-up of $11,750, instead of the $8,500 that applies from age 50.
The plan has you retiring at 63, so you would have 2 years without Medicare before age 65.
Medicare starts at 65, and if you miss your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, a monthly late penalty can apply for as long as you have Part B.

finding.headline: About 17 cents of each dollar you earn goes to tax now; about 8 cents in retirement.
details: Now you pay about 17% of your pay in tax, including payroll tax. In retirement, withdrawals would be taxed at about 8%.

Draw on taxable savings first, then the 401(k) and other pre-tax accounts, and Roth accounts last. Your savings are about 69% pre-tax, 26% Roth, and 5% taxable or cash, so most of your money will be taxed when you take it out.
This is a rough guide, not tax advice. Talk with a tax professional before you change how you save or withdraw.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $31,427 a year: $4,400 into a 401(k) or IRA, $27,027 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.

Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $57,100 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 67 for you and 70 for your partner, which pays about $64,600 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $38,800 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay and the child tax credit applies. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 95. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
